h1: Choosing wine glasses without buying a full cabinet of them
title: How to Choose Wine Glasses | Craft Beer School
desc: Which wine glasses you actually need at home: shape, size, stems, sparkling glasses and how to care for them in an Indian kitchen.
teaser: You do not need a different glass for every grape. One good shape covers almost everything.
standfirst: Wine glass shops would like you to buy a glass for every grape. You can enjoy almost any wine from one well chosen shape. Here is what matters and what does not.
sections:
A wine glass does three jobs. It holds the wine. It traps aroma above the surface so you can smell it. It lets you swirl without spilling, which releases more aroma.

Shape changes what you smell more than most people expect. Pour the same wine into a tumbler and a tulip glass and the difference is obvious within a minute. That is why the bowl matters more than anything else. A bowl that is wider at the bottom and narrower at the rim lets aroma build up and funnels it towards your nose. A straight-sided tumbler lets it drift away. Brewers will recognise the idea from our beer glassware guide, where tulip shapes do the same job for aromatic beers.
The one glass that covers most wines

Start with six glasses rather than a dozen. Breakage is part of owning glassware and a small set is cheaper to replace with the same design. If you buy one set, buy a medium-sized tulip-shaped glass with a stem, holding roughly 350 to 450 ml when full. You pour only a third of that, so the wine has room to move.

This glass works for whites, rosé, light and medium reds and even sparkling wine. Many professional tasters use a version of it. The international standard tasting glass, defined in ISO 3591, is a smaller tulip that judges and trainers use precisely because it is neutral across styles.
When a second shape is worth it

• Larger red glass. If you drink a lot of full-bodied reds, a wider bowl gives more surface area and room to swirl. It is pleasant, not essential.
  • Sparkling. Tall narrow flutes keep bubbles longer but hide aroma. Many winemakers now prefer a tulip or white wine glass for good sparkling wine. A flute is fine for a party toast.
  • Small dessert glass. Sweet and fortified wines are poured in small measures, so a small tulip suits them.

Beyond that, grape-specific glasses are a refinement for collectors. Our guide to red, white, rosé and sparkling wine explains the style differences that drive these shapes.
Details that matter more than brand

• Size. Too small and you cannot swirl. Too large and the glass is fragile and hard to store. The middle of the range is the sensible buy.
  • Thin rim. A thin, cut rim lets the wine flow smoothly onto the tongue. Thick rolled rims feel clumsy.
  • Stem. Holding the stem keeps your hand from warming the wine. That matters more in an Indian summer than in a cool European dining room.
  • Clear and plain. Coloured or heavily cut glass hides the colour of the wine.
  • Glass or crystal. Lead-free crystal can be thinner and stronger than ordinary glass. Good soda-lime glass is perfectly adequate and cheaper to replace.
Caring for glasses in an Indian kitchen

Indian kitchens are hard on glassware. Cooking oil hangs in the air, spice tins sit close by and hard borewell water leaves spots. The biggest enemy of a wine glass is not breakage. It is residue. Detergent film, oil from a kitchen towel or the smell of a cupboard all change what you taste.

  • Wash in hot water with very little detergent, then rinse well.
  • If you use a dishwasher, choose a gentle cycle and skip rinse aid if it leaves a film.
  • Dry and polish with a lint-free cloth kept only for glasses.
  • Store upright in a closed cabinet, away from spice tins and cooking smells. Glasses stored upside down on a shelf can pick up a musty note.

Before pouring, sniff the empty glass. If it smells of anything at all, rinse it.

Chill whites and sparkling wine in the fridge, not in the glass. Skip the ice unless you are making a spritzer on purpose, because melting ice dilutes the wine within minutes. Pour no more than a third full. Hold the stem. Swirl gently on the table if you are not used to it, then smell before you sip. Our guide to wine tasting for beginners walks through what to look for.

Once you notice how much a glass changes the aroma, the next question tends to be why the wine smells the way it does at all. That comes down to the grape and how it was made.
faqs: Do I need separate glasses for red and white wine?
No. A medium tulip-shaped glass works well for both. A larger bowl for big reds is a nice extra, not a necessity.
Are flutes the best glass for sparkling wine?
They keep bubbles longer but trap less aroma. Many people prefer a white wine glass for good sparkling wine and keep flutes for toasts.
Why does my wine smell odd in some glasses?
Usually detergent residue, cloth lint or cupboard smells. Rinse with hot water and polish with a clean, lint-free cloth.
